On move 130, black made the losing blunder Qe6. Which of the following queen moves could black have played to draw the game?


Answer Choices:
A. Qa1
B. Qa7
C. Qg2
D. Qf2
E. Qb2
F. Qd2
G. Qa6
H. Qh2
I. Qa8
J. Qa5
K. Qa4
L. Qc2
M. Qe2
N. Qa3

1.text:
In the position after 129… Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the only White material that can
ever get at the queen is the R f5.  After 130 Kh3 the R f5 is still
hanging to the Ng3 and the 5th rank is closed on the a–f line by the
white e5 pawn.  In particular the queen is safe as long as she stays on
the a–file up to the a4 pawn and she stays on the 2nd rank, because from
there she can always come back to the a-file and she can keep the
perpetual h1/h2 – g2 resource against the White K h3.

The blunder 130… Qe6 puts the queen on the diagonal f5–e6–g4–h3 and
allows White to gain the tempo Kh4 and then to force the queen into the
net.  The normal drawing way to keep the tempi is to keep the queen on
the a–file, i.e. to retreat to a1.  130… Qa1! puts the queen on the a-
file again, with

* 131… Qh1+ 132 Kg4 Qg2+ 133 Kh5 Qh3+ etc.

a perpetual and with the R f5 never able to get at a queen which is
still more than one file away from the blocked a5 square.  130… Qa3
is the same idea on the a-file, the only other legal a-file retreat
with a4 occupied by the black a-pawn, and the 2nd-rank retreats
Qb2/Qc2/Qd2/Qe2 are the same idea on the 2nd rank.  Of the moves
quoted in the list the canonical drawing retreat is

A. Qa1

which is the usual form in which the draw is quoted, Qa3 being the
same a-file idea.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: F. Qd2

The drawing resource is 130...Qd2! Black needs to keep the queen on the second rank, where it attacks the important f4-pawn and controls key checking diagonals. After 131.Kh4, Black has 131...Qxf4+ and can follow with a perpetual against the exposed white king. If White instead tries 131.e6, then 131...Qd6 holds the position by blockading the e-pawn and keeping the queen active. The move played, 130...Qe6, allowed White to play Kh4 and Nh5 with tempo, after which the e- and f-pawns decide the game. So 130...Qd2 would have been the drawing queen move.

2.text:
After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the white king is on h3, the white rook is on
f5, the white knight is on g3 and the white e–pawn is on e5.  The only
real threat is  e6 with e7-e8=Q.  The queen is on a2 and can give an
immediate check on the h–file / g–file

* 130... Qe6+  is the check which Nepomniachtchi played.  It is a
check on the a2–e6–h3 diagonal and it does block the e–pawn for the
moment, but after 131 Kh4 Qh6+ 132 Nh5 Qh7 133 e6 the queen is too far
away to stop the e–pawn and White wins.

The queen can keep the position in zugzwang and can even force a
perpetual by a check on the 2nd rank.  From a2 the only checking
squares which are on the list are

* a2–g2+ ,  a2–h2+ .

In particular the classic perpetual is

130... Qh2+

1... Qh2+ 1.Kg4 Qg2+ 2.Kh4 Qh2+ etc.  The same idea is available as
130... Qg2+ , 1.Kxg2 Rxf7+ etc., i.e. a perpetual check on the
h3–g2–h2 line.  That is the normal drawing defence to 130.Kh3,
the 130...Qe6+ check being the losing blunder.  The usual textbook
perpetual quoted for the position is the 130...Qh2+ check, essentially
the same as the 130...Qg2+ check.

5.text:
In the line that is actually played the queen is already on a2

    White Kg2 – Black Qb3 – White Rd5 – White Re5+ – White Rf5+ – White e5
    Black Qa2+ White Kh3

and White has the two rooks on d5 and f5, N g3, e5 etc.  After
1…Qe6 the queen walks on to the long a2–e6 diagonal which is now
open because the White d5 rook is taken off the diagonal by the
text book mate

    131 Rg5+ Kh4 132 Re5+ etc.

and the game is lost for Black.  The point of the position is that
with the king on h3 the a–file is the only file on which the queen can
stay out of the mating net.  As long as the queen remains on the a–file
White has no immediate mate and in fact Black can keep the
perpetual by continual checks on the second rank.  In particular

    130… Qa1

keeps the queen on the a–file, and with it the whole family

    130… Qa3 Qa4 Qa5 Qa6 Qa7 Qa8

keeps the draw.  The move that is usually quoted is the most
economical 130… Qa1, after which White has no forced win and Black
can draw by repetition.  This is the move that is normally given
as the drawing resource; any a–file retreat has the same effect.
The move actually played 130… Qe6 is the losing blunder.

3.text:
In the position after  129... Qa2+ 130.Kh3 the black queen is already on
the a–file and the white king is on h3

* Kg3 is occupied by the white N, * Kg2 and Kh4 are covered by the
queen on h2 and the rook can no longer be used to stop the queen
check.

The only way to gain the tempo that is needed to stop the e–pawn
going to e6/e7/e8 is to check at once.  From a2 the two squares
which really check the king on h3 are

h2 :  Qa2–h2+      and      g2 :  Qa2–g2+

in particular

 130… Qh2+ 131.Kg4 Qg3+ 132.Kh4 Qh3+ 133.Kg5 Qg4+ …

is the familiar perpetual on the h–/g–files.  The same idea is
obtained with the essentially symmetrical check

 130… Qg2+ 131.Kh4 Qh2+ …

which is the drawing perpetual that is normally quoted in the
analysis.  The move actually played 130…Qe6 is illegal in the
strict sense – the queen would stand on the e–file with the black
king on e8 – and in any case it loses the perpetual and lets White
promote.

That is the Qh2+ drawing perpetual, the Qg2+ check being the
symmetrical perpetual.  In the lettering of the list this is

H. Qh2

with the essentially equivalent Qg2+ C. Qg2+ also leading to a
draw by perpetual.

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The position after 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is White Kg2–>Kh3, N g3, e5, Rf5/Rd5 and Black Ke8, Qa2. White’s immediate winning idea is e6–e7=Q with the king on h3 being too far away to stop the promotion. Tempo is therefore everything for Black.

From a2 the squares that give an immediate check to Kh3 are the
rank-3 squares a3/b3, the diagonal e6, the file h squares h2 and the
diagonal g2/f1 squares. In practice the only forcing drawing
resources are the checks on the h-/g-files which give the familiar
Kg4–Kh4–Kg5 perpetual on the 2nd rank.

* 130…Qh2+ is the textbook perpetual. 131 Kg4 Qg2+ 132 Kh4 Qh2+ etc.
keeps the king tied up and stops e6. The symmetric 130…Qg2+ gives the
same idea 131 Kh4 Qh2+ and is essentially the same perpetual.
These are the checking drawing resources quoted in the game notes.

The a-file quiet retreats are the other family mentioned in the
deliberation. Keeping the queen on the a-file, e.g. 130…Qa1, keeps the
queen out of the rook net and allows Black to re-enter the h1–h2
checking net on the next move, so a-file moves are often quoted as
drawing as well. In the list the a-file moves that are actually legal
in the diagram are Qa1 and Qa3; Qa4– Qa8 are blocked by the Black
a-pawn on a4. Moves Qa7/Qa5/Qa6/Qa8 are illegal for that reason.

The second-rank quiet moves Qb2/Qc2/Qd2/Qe2/Qf2 are not checking and
do not stop e6 quickly enough, and F. Qd2 is not the canonical
perpetual. The blunder 130…Qe6+ is a check on the a2–e6–h3 diagonal
but it walks the queen onto the e-file and lets White gain the tempo
Kh4 Nh5 with e6 decisive.

Hence the forcing drawing checks are the Qh2+ perpetual, essentially
the same as Qg2+, with the a-file retreat Qa1 – and the essentially
equivalent Qa3 – being the quiet drawing ideas that are also cited.
If a single canonical move is required it is the perpetual check
H. Qh2, with C. Qg2+ the symmetric equivalent. A. Qa1 is the quiet
a-file drawing retreat most often quoted in the literature.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The position after 129…Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is the well known
perpetual / promotion net of Game 6. White has K h3, Ng3, Rf5, e5,f4,h4
against… Ke8 and Qa2. The only real White threat is  e6-e7-e8=Q and
the only Black resource is to keep the queen active enough to keep the
king in check and to stop the e-pawn from running.

From a2 the queen can stay on the a-file or come down to the 2nd rank.
The queen on a1 is on the a1-e5 diagonal so that 130…Qa1 immediately
attacks the e5 pawn.  After 130…Qa1 White cannot just play e6 for free
and the same a1-h1 line gives the normal perpetual

130…Qa1 131 e6 Qh1+ 132 Kg4 Qg1+ 133 Kh4 Qh3+ …

etc.  The same idea is the a-file retreat that is normally quoted as
130…Qa3, and indeed 130…Qa3 controls e7, a4 controls e8 and a1
controls e5, so that the promotion chain is stopped and a perpetual on
the h/g-files can be kept.  In the literature the move is usually
given in the canonical form 130…Qa1, 130…Qa3 being the same a-file
defence.

The rank-2 retreats Qb2/Qc2/Qd2/Qe2 are the same family of keeping the
queen on the second rank in order to attack e5 / keep checking
diagonals and are frequently mentioned as drawing.  The immediate
checks Qa2-h2+ and Qa2-g2+ are losing because the queen is adjacent to
the h3 king and can be taken by Kxh2 / Kxg2 with no protection, so the
H. Qh2 / C. Qg2 perpetuals quoted by colleagues 2-3 are not viable.
F. Qd2 is a second rank move that does not attack e5 and is not the
canonical drawing resource.

On balance the textbook drawing resource is the a-file retreat, most
often quoted as A. Qa1, with the equivalent and often cited 130…Qa3
N. Qa3 and the other a-file squares that keep the queen active being
the same idea.  That is the move that is conventionally given as the
draw after 130 Kh3, rather than the losing 130…Qe6.

5.text:
After 129... Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the queen is still the only thing which keeps
the e-pawn under control.  As long as the queen can stay on the a–file
it can keep the e–pawn in check and it can always come back to the
second rank for a perpetual on the h–/g–files.

The move which is normally quoted as the drawing resource is the
a–file retreat

* 130… Qa1 !

which keeps the queen on the a–file.  With the queen on the a–file
White has no immediate win on e6/e7 and Black can keep the
perpetual e.g.

131 Kh4 Qh1+ 132 Kg5 Qg1+ …

The essentially equivalent a–file retreats Qa3, Qa4 … and the second–
rank retreats Qb2/Qc2/Qd2/Qe2 are the same idea.  In particular the
immediate perpetual checks

130… Qh2+ 131 Kg4 Qg2+ 132 Kh4 Qh3+ …  and  the symmetric
130… Qg2+

are the same drawing idea.  This is the move which is quoted in the
literature as the normal drawing retreat, 130… Qa1 !, Qa3 being the
same a–file idea.  The perpetual check which is most often quoted is

H. Qh2+

and the symmetric Qg2+ C.  Qg2+, the textbook a–file retreat being
A. Qa1, with N. Qa3 the same idea.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion has shifted from the initial idea that any a-file retreat works to a more concrete
board-state check. After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the white king is on h3, the white rook is on f5, the
white knight is on g3 and the white e-pawn is on e5.  The black pawn is already on a3 from
43…a3, so the a-file is blocked upwards: a3 is occupied by own pawn and a4-a8 are
unreachable from a2.  The only a-file queen move that is still legal from a2 is
A. Qa1.  All moves Qa3-Qa8 are illegal because of the own pawn on a3.

Rank 2 is now free – the rook that was on d2 in move 125 has been moved d2-d5-e5-f5
on moves 126-128 – so the queen can in fact use the whole 2nd rank b2-h2.  That makes
the Qh2+/Qg2+ ideas legally reachable, but the immediate checks are adjacent to the
king on h3 and the queen on h2/g2 is not obviously protected, so the “perpetual” that
colleagues 2-3 quote is in fact very close to Kxh2/Kxg2.

What is essential for the draw is to keep a checking tempo against the e5–e8 promotion.
If the queen stays on the a-file or on the 2nd rank it can always come back to a
checking square on the 3rd rank/file h/diagonal g2 in one move after White plays e6.
Hence the family of second-rank retreats

* E. Qb2 → …Qb3+,
* L. Qc2 → …Qc3+,
* F. Qd2 → …Qd3+,
* M. Qe2 → …Qe3+,
* D. Qf2 → …Qf3+

all preserve a one-move checking resource and therefore delay the promotion.
A. Qa1 is the canonical form of the same idea, a1→c3+ etc., and is the move most
often quoted in the literature.  The a-file moves B Qa7, G Qa6, I Qa8, J Qa5, K Qa4
and the immediate a3 check N Qa3 are illegal because of the own pawn on a3.

Moves C Qg2 and H Qh2 are now legally reachable on the 2nd rank, and they are the
immediate-check variants that colleagues 2-3 discuss.  In practice they are the most
famous perpetual candidates, 130…Qh2+ 131 Kg4 Qg3+ etc.; Qg2+ is the symmetric
check and is normally quoted together with Qh2+.

The non-drawing / illegal options in the list are the a-file moves beyond a1
blocked by the a3 pawn, and the immediate checks Qg2/Qh2 are the contentious
perpetual candidates.  The safest, universally cited drawing resource among the
legal options is the a1 retreat A Qa1, with the equivalent second-rank
retreats E Qb2, L Qc2, F Qd2, M Qe2, D Qf2 also preserving the draw.  This reconciles
Colleague 1/5’s a-file retreat with Colleagues 2-3’s perpetual-check idea, once the
a3 pawn block and the rook’s move from d2 to f5 are taken into account.

The position after 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is White Kg2–>Kh3, N g3, e5, Rf5/Rd5 and Black Ke8, Qa2. White’s immediate winning idea is e6–e7=Q with the king on h3 being too far away to stop the promotion. Tempo is therefore everything for Black.

From a2 the squares that give an immediate check to Kh3 are the
rank-3 squares a3/b3, the diagonal e6, the file h squares h2 and the
diagonal g2/f1 squares. In practice the only forcing drawing
resources are the checks on the h-/g-files which give the familiar
Kg4–Kh4–Kg5 perpetual on the 2nd rank.

* 130…Qh2+ is the textbook perpetual. 131 Kg4 Qg2+ 132 Kh4 Qh2+ etc.
keeps the king tied up and stops e6. The symmetric 130…Qg2+ gives the
same idea 131 Kh4 Qh2+ and is essentially the same perpetual.
These are the checking drawing resources quoted in the game notes.

The a-file quiet retreats are the other family mentioned in the
deliberation. Keeping the queen on the a-file, e.g. 130…Qa1, keeps the
queen out of the rook net and allows Black to re-enter the h1–h2
checking net on the next move, so a-file moves are often quoted as
drawing as well. In the list the a-file moves that are actually legal
in the diagram are Qa1 and Qa3; Qa4– Qa8 are blocked by the Black
a-pawn on a4. Moves Qa7/Qa5/Qa6/Qa8 are illegal for that reason.

The second-rank quiet moves Qb2/Qc2/Qd2/Qe2/Qf2 are not checking and
do not stop e6 quickly enough, and F. Qd2 is not the canonical
perpetual. The blunder 130…Qe6+ is a check on the a2–e6–h3 diagonal
but it walks the queen onto the e-file and lets White gain the tempo
Kh4 Nh5 with e6 decisive.

Hence the forcing drawing checks are the Qh2+ perpetual, essentially
the same as Qg2+, with the a-file retreat Qa1 – and the essentially
equivalent Qa3 – being the quiet drawing ideas that are also cited.
If a single canonical move is required it is the perpetual check
H. Qh2, with C. Qg2+ the symmetric equivalent. A. Qa1 is the quiet
a-file drawing retreat most often quoted in the literature.
reflection_text.2:
The position after 129…Qa2+ 130 Kh3 is the well known
perpetual / promotion net of Game 6. White has K h3, Ng3, Rf5, e5,f4,h4
against… Ke8 and Qa2. The only real White threat is  e6-e7-e8=Q and
the only Black resource is to keep the queen active enough to keep the
king in check and to stop the e-pawn from running.

From a2 the queen can stay on the a-file or come down to the 2nd rank.
The queen on a1 is on the a1-e5 diagonal so that 130…Qa1 immediately
attacks the e5 pawn.  After 130…Qa1 White cannot just play e6 for free
and the same a1-h1 line gives the normal perpetual

130…Qa1 131 e6 Qh1+ 132 Kg4 Qg1+ 133 Kh4 Qh3+ …

etc.  The same idea is the a-file retreat that is normally quoted as
130…Qa3, and indeed 130…Qa3 controls e7, a4 controls e8 and a1
controls e5, so that the promotion chain is stopped and a perpetual on
the h/g-files can be kept.  In the literature the move is usually
given in the canonical form 130…Qa1, 130…Qa3 being the same a-file
defence.

The rank-2 retreats Qb2/Qc2/Qd2/Qe2 are the same family of keeping the
queen on the second rank in order to attack e5 / keep checking
diagonals and are frequently mentioned as drawing.  The immediate
checks Qa2-h2+ and Qa2-g2+ are losing because the queen is adjacent to
the h3 king and can be taken by Kxh2 / Kxg2 with no protection, so the
H. Qh2 / C. Qg2 perpetuals quoted by colleagues 2-3 are not viable.
F. Qd2 is a second rank move that does not attack e5 and is not the
canonical drawing resource.

On balance the textbook drawing resource is the a-file retreat, most
often quoted as A. Qa1, with the equivalent and often cited 130…Qa3
N. Qa3 and the other a-file squares that keep the queen active being
the same idea.  That is the move that is conventionally given as the
draw after 130 Kh3, rather than the losing 130…Qe6.

are the same drawing idea.  This is the move which is quoted in the

reflection_text.3:
The discussion has shifted from the initial idea that any a-file retreat works to a more concrete
board-state check. After 129 e5 Qa2+ 130 Kh3 the white king is on h3, the white rook is on f5, the
white knight is on g3 and the white e-pawn is on e5.  The black pawn is already on a3 from
43…a3, so the a-file is blocked upwards: a3 is occupied by own pawn and a4-a8 are
unreachable from a2.  The only a-file queen move that is still legal from a2 is
A. Qa1.  All moves Qa3-Qa8 are illegal because of the own pawn on a3.

Rank 2 is now free – the rook that was on d2 in move 125 has been moved d2-d5-e5-f5
on moves 126-128 – so the queen can in fact use the whole 2nd rank b2-h2.  That makes
the Qh2+/Qg2+ ideas legally reachable, but the immediate checks are adjacent to the
king on h3 and the queen on h2/g2 is not obviously protected, so the “perpetual” that
colleagues 2-3 quote is in fact very close to Kxh2/Kxg2.

What is essential for the draw is to keep a checking tempo against the e5–e8 promotion.
If the queen stays on the a-file or on the 2nd rank it can always come back to a
checking square on the 3rd rank/file h/diagonal g2 in one move after White plays e6.
Hence the family of second-rank retreats

* E. Qb2 → …Qb3+,
* L. Qc2 → …Qc3+,
* F. Qd2 → …Qd3+,
* M. Qe2 → …Qe3+,
* D. Qf2 → …Qf3+

all preserve a one-move checking resource and therefore delay the promotion.
A. Qa1 is the canonical form of the same idea, a1→c3+ etc., and is the move most
often quoted in the literature.  The a-file moves B Qa7, G Qa6, I Qa8, J Qa5, K Qa4
and the immediate a3 check N Qa3 are illegal because of the own pawn on a3.

Moves C Qg2 and H Qh2 are now legally reachable on the 2nd rank, and they are the
immediate-check variants that colleagues 2-3 discuss.  In practice they are the most
famous perpetual candidates, 130…Qh2+ 131 Kg4 Qg3+ etc.; Qg2+ is the symmetric
check and is normally quoted together with Qh2+.

The non-drawing / illegal options in the list are the a-file moves beyond a1
blocked by the a3 pawn, and the immediate checks Qg2/Qh2 are the contentious
perpetual candidates.  The safest, universally cited drawing resource among the
legal options is the a1 retreat A Qa1, with the equivalent second-rank
retreats E Qb2, L Qc2, F Qd2, M Qe2, D Qf2 also preserving the draw.  This reconciles
Colleague 1/5’s a-file retreat with Colleagues 2-3’s perpetual-check idea, once the
a3 pawn block and the rook’s move from d2 to f5 are taken into account.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m with C1/C5 here: **A. Qa1** is the clean drawing retreat. The key is that White’s main winning idea is the e-pawn advance, and 130...Qe6 fails because it moves the queen off the checking network and lets White gain the Kh4/Nh5/e6 tempo.

After **130...Qa1**, Black keeps the queen on the a-file and preserves the Qh1+ resource after White tries e6, so the e-pawn cannot simply run. I also think the proposed **Qh2+ / Qg2+** perpetuals are not sound: from a2 to h2 or g2, the queen lands on a square controlled by the white king on h3, so White can simply **131.Kxh2** or **131.Kxg2** and win the queen. That is not a drawing perpetual.

**Qd2** also looks less convincing because it is not a check and does not address the e6 tempo in the same forcing way. Among the a-file moves, Qa1 is more precise than Qa3 because the queen on a3 has its line toward h3 blocked by the white knight on g3, so Black loses the immediate Qh1+ resource.

So the move I would back is **A. Qa1**.
